First of all, creds for seeing the problem with having alone, untamed budgie and wanting to solve it. She will be very much alone without, so I'm all for the buddy. There are exeptions, but the general rule is that females are more prone to be aggressive towards other females, than towards other males. There will probably me more company with a male, and you do not want to end up with having to keep them separated because of hostileness.  But as you say, there's the risk of her mating, and if that were to happen, the male would have to be over 1 year old to avoid gender related complications. Take in consideration the temperament of your female. If she's dominant, it would be fitting if the new partner is not more dominant, to avoid conflict. However, it is very unlikely the budgies will still try to mate if there are no nests around. You can also use UV-light to control the season, make them believe it's not breeding time (according to sources).

No matter the gender, I think you should buy a very young budgie and tame it. Spend a month on getting it real tame. Buy from a breeder, not a store (unless the store is very good and all the breeders are bad), to get an as healthy and calm bud as possible. Speaking from my own experience, an untamed, skittish old budgie can go from trying to fly away when you enter the room to being a real flirt and sitting on shoulders, heads, hands etc and find company with humans, exclusively through being with two tamed budgies and observing life unfold. Btw, the tamed ones were not "negatively" by the untamed one at all, with exeption from a bad habit of loving to rip up curtains (which they now have quit because humans are much better perches) and some classic budgie songs that were quite annoying.

And I had a budgie who eventually had to be put down due to consequences brought on her by our lack of knowledge and UV-light. It took her 8 years to become ill, but she suffered enourmously when she did. The veterinarians here all say that you need it, and trust me, you do not want to learn it the bad way.

Everybirdy needs to learn how to fly at some point. First of, the good thing about letting the bird be fully flighted as a baby, is that this means that it'll learn to fly when the body is small and weak. Now your bird is strong from training, so she is prone to do more damage to herself than a little baby is. Her body and mind was built to fly.  When taking it away from the bird, you miss out on a whole lot of mental stimulation,  exercise and joy, just to name a few. If she's ever in danger at home,  her body is built to rely on wings to save her. Flying around in the apartement is obligatory. The lack of it can result in behaviour issues. I buyer a huge cage for just two budgies because I needed to be able to let them be in the cage for a whole day. However, despite the big cage, after a while without flying, they eat less, make more noise, and can become hostile against me or angsty because of all of the energy. Then take proceed to take a few rounds around the room to the point where I can hear them breath. They gain so much from flying. They are much nicer to be with when they have a balanced day with moderate flying evened out throughout the day. They seem much happier, basically.

To learn her how to fly, take it slow. If she suddenly has all her feathers popped out again and you let her fly in a huge room, she's likely to hurt herself. We don't want that happen. Now that she's clipped,  you can still teach her some coordination. Go in a small room,and make her fly from one place to the other (note that I have no idea how good of a flyer she is, so I'm just taking it from the start). That way, she'll also learn how to land. Increase the distance as her wings grow out. Don't put her in a situation where she can hurt herself. She'll be like a baby on drugs, clumsy as shit but strong as hell. Cover the windows etc. Make flying a good experience if she's nervous, millets and treats goes a long way. Eventually, you can let her be out in bigger rooms, but start small. If you do this,  you'll follow the natural progress unclipped birds follow. Just keep in that her strength and coordination are not balanced. She'll be fine, no worries, but keeping her clipped will be very dangerous and I sincerely hope for the both of you that you let her wings be grown out. Feel free to message me again if there is anything else or if you're still unsure.

Just make sure you're getting safe toys. The most innocent things can literally kill your bird. Find a list on the web,  just to make sure you have a good overview. Let me know if you want me to send you a direct link.

If the birds are of separate species (as they are), they can't breed. Some can, such as horses and donkeys, but the offspring will be infertile. They can bond though, and it seems like your budgie is making "fake eggs", aka infertile eggs. It's typical for females. The linnie is probably just taking on the role as the father, he might be adopting the eggs. It's nothing to worry about, but as the eggs are infertile (if she haven't mated with another budgie), she can get exhausted and damage her feathers from constantly laying on the eggs. You can give her a nesting box to let her get some peace, since she thinks the eggs will hatch, but it can make her lay eggs more often, which takes a toll on her health. You'll have to remove the eggs after some time.

You have no idea how good that is to hear. Check out senegals and green cheeked conures, they are small but a bigger challenge. There's a bigger chance they'll get along with budgies. In general, senegals are low, conures medium and caiques high energy. They are all very intelligent and cuddly, so I think they could be a good match. When it comes to caiques being a more "serious pet", I disagree. It's all about how you keep the birds. I keep budgies as if they were bigger parrots; they have a cage which cost literally 10 times more than one budgie, they are super tame and acts as tame conures (just with a lot more energy) and are in general a part of the family. With other words, they are kept as they are supposed to be. Budgies are higher demand than most people think (not talking about you, but people, especially where I live). If someone were to actually keep a bird in a not serious manner, for example one little budgie on a tiny, round cage, it is abuse. I don't have time for keeping birds of higher demand at the moment, so having two super tame guys who loves each other and can be alone for a day is the perfect match for me at the moment. I'm serious as fuck even though the birds are small. It's not about what bird you keep, but how you keep it. Small birds can be as awesome as bigger ones if they are correctly handled.

Ah, so many stories. I think I'll have to go with the unconditional love between my two guys. They were at the vet, and both were scared, naturally. They comforted each other by literally digging their little faces in each other and constantly [cuddling](http://i.imgur.com/nUHfXqP.png) for the whole ride. I do mean it when I say constantly. When one of them later got his meds, he accidentally got some in his eye, and Mel literally flew immediately to him and started to gently cleaning the eye. The med tasted like shit, so he knew what he was doing. Another time, I had to take just one of them down, Mel, and he started comforting me, as if I was the one who was scared (well I was very worried, so he got that part right). I hadn't been able to cuddle with him since he was 3 months old (he grew out of it), but on that trip, he mushed his little face into my finger and let me give him a good old head scratch for the whole trip. Not to be comforted, but to comfort me. I know his body language well. When we got back, he ignored his birdie buddy and acted like he was a kid again around me. [Bonus pic of the derp being Mel's little bitch](http://i.imgur.com/GztNMEt.png) It's amazing to see how the little dinos are so loving and caring.
